_readme: PMS Training Pop Quiz question bank. Only days that carry an assessment in the training plan appear here — the portal mirrors the plan. Days 1, 9, 11, 13, 14, 15, 16 and 21 are assessed by deliverables, role-plays or shadow sessions instead, so they are deliberately absent. Schema matches the PMA app: mcq (answer = index), multi (answer = array of indices), fill (accept = array of strings). 'explain' renders as HTML on the review screen.

2.title: Day 2 — Strategy Foundations
2.sub: Goals, funnel types, awareness stages, PMS scope. ~12 min.

questions.prompt: A PMA keeps rebuilding the campaign — switching ABO to CBO, re-splitting ad sets, renaming things — but results stay flat. Per AdClass's core belief, where is the real problem most likely hiding?
options: The CBO vs. ABO structure
The creative and the offer
The number of ad sets
The bid strategy
questions.explain: Campaign structure is only ~10–20% of results — the other 80–90% is creative and offer. If reorganizing the account isn't moving the needle, stop: fix the creative, offer, funnel, or data. As the guide puts it, “if creative can't solve it, it's an economics problem.”

questions.prompt: Three creative rounds in and a flat account still hasn't moved. Campaign structure is only ~10–20% of the result, so what are you actually checking next?
options: The campaign structure — ABO vs CBO, how the ad sets are split
Audience targeting and the lookalike seeds
The offer and the funnel economics — if creative can't solve it, it's an economics problem
Bid strategy and budget pacing
questions.explain: Creative is the biggest lever but it isn't infinite. When genuinely good creative stops moving an account, the constraint is upstream — the offer, the price, or the funnel's ability to convert. Reorganising the account is the 10–20%, and a fourth creative round is usually money spent avoiding the harder conversation.

questions.prompt: An account has one winning ad carrying almost all the spend and no new concepts launched in three weeks. Which of the three pillars is it actually failing on?
options: Creative Diversity — everything rests on one concept, so there's nothing to fall back to
Angle Testing
Scaling Winners
Budget Pacing
questions.explain: The three pillars are Creative Diversity, Angle Testing and Scaling Winners. Angle testing is the upstream cause and worth fixing too, but the immediate failure is concentration: one ad carrying the account means the day it tires, the account stops. Budget Pacing isn't one of the three.

questions.prompt: A new client sells a $6K done-with-you programme and closes on a 45-minute call. Which of the four core funnel types is the default here?
options: Low-ticket funnel — the purchase closes inside the funnel
Lead-magnet funnel — collect the email first, then nurture to a call
Webinar funnel — a live event warms them before the call
VSL funnel — long-form video does the selling and books the call
questions.explain: High-ticket and call-closed means VSL. Low-ticket is for offers that complete on-site, so the price point rules it out. Lead-magnet adds a step that costs call volume. A webinar is genuinely viable at this price, which makes it the defensible second answer — it's just heavier to run and usually earns its place on a launch rather than evergreen.

questions.prompt: In a lead-magnet funnel, the prospect opts in for a free resource. How do those leads typically get converted into customers?
options: An outbound call — reps call the leads, supported by email nurture
They check out for the product right there in the funnel
They're sent straight to a live webinar to buy
A retargeting ad closes them automatically
questions.explain: In a lead-magnet funnel (Ad → opt-in → deliver), the “call” usually becomes outbound — reps call the leads — supported by email nurture. You trade a low-friction opt-in for contact info, then do the selling afterward. (Contrast: the low-ticket funnel closes the purchase in-funnel with no call.)

questions.prompt: You'd normally optimise a book-a-call funnel for the Schedule event. On a new account, when would you deliberately not do that?
options: When the client would rather see more leads than more calls
When the account can't produce enough Schedule events for the algorithm to learn — optimise one step earlier until volume supports it
Never — Schedule is always the correct event on a call funnel
When CPMs are running high
questions.explain: The rule is the furthest-along event you can get volume on. Below the learning threshold you're starving the algorithm and buying noise, so you step back to Lead and move up once volume allows. Note what doesn't change the answer: what the client would prefer to look at, and CPMs.

questions.prompt: A problem-aware prospect knows they have a problem but doesn't yet know solutions exist. Which ad headline is aimed at them?
options: “See why agents are leaving [Competitor] for our listing system”
“The real reason your listings keep going stale (and it's not your photos)”
“You've watched the demo — here's 20% off, this week only”
“Book your strategy call — only 3 slots left”
questions.explain: Problem-aware headlines agitate the problem and stir curiosity without naming a solution (lead-magnet / educational territory). Comparing named solutions = solution-aware; direct CTAs to people who already know you = most-aware.

questions.prompt: Your client's audience already knows programs like theirs exist and is actively comparing a few options before buying. Which awareness stage are they in — and what funnel territory does that point to?
options: Problem-aware → lead magnet / educational content
Solution-aware → VSL / webinar / application
Most aware → retargeting / direct CTA
Unaware → broad brand-awareness content
questions.explain: Solution-aware = knows solutions exist and is comparing options → VSL / webinar / application territory. Compare problem-aware (knows the problem, not that solutions exist) → lead-magnet / educational territory. Each stage maps to a different funnel and a different optimization event.

questions.prompt: An account is stuck and has only tested 4 creative angles in the last 30 days. Which play does it need first?
options: Just raise the budgets
Play 2: Better funnel for cold traffic
Play 1: More, better ads (Creative Diversity)
Play 3: Add a new platform (Google/YouTube)
questions.explain: The ladder is in strict order. Step 1: have you genuinely tested 10+ angles in 30 days? Four isn't enough, so the fix is Play 1 — more, better ads. Most stuck accounts haven't actually finished Play 1.

questions.prompt: On a pod, which set of responsibilities belongs to the PMS (not the PMA)?
options: Building and launching campaigns and running daily in-account optimization
Strategy before the click — funnel, messaging, angles — plus owning the client relationship and the pod's plan
Editing and producing the creative
Running the prospect's sales calls
questions.explain: The PMS owns strategy, the client relationship, and the pod's plan. Campaign build and daily in-account work is the PMA's; creative production and sales calls sit elsewhere entirely.

questions.tag: Day 2 · Core belief, in client language
questions.prompt: A client wants you to 'just fix the targeting' on a flat account. Which response is both correct and client-ready?
options: 'Sure, we'll rebuild the targeting this week.'
'Targeting doesn't matter at all.'
'The account is fine — give it time.'
'Targeting and structure are only ~10–20% of the result — the bigger levers are creative and offer, so here's the plan to test new angles.'
questions.explain: Applies the 10/90 belief and translates it for a client. Agreeing to rebuild targeting spends a week on the small lever; dismissing targeting outright is wrong and sounds it; 'give it time' is not a plan.

3.title: Day 3 — Ad Auditing
3.sub: Diagnosing why an account is stuck — before you touch anything. ~12 min.

questions.prompt: Select the three patterns of accounts that stop scaling.
options: The ceiling account
The slow-rot account
The over-reliant account
The saturation account
The runaway account
questions.explain: The three: ceiling (stuck ~$4–5K/day, falls apart when pushed), slow-rot (surface metrics fine, lead quality declining for months), over-reliant (one ad/funnel/style carrying everything). “Saturation” and “runaway” aren't AdClass terms.

questions.prompt: An account's surface numbers look fine — CTR is steady, cost per lead is flat — but the sales team has complained for months that lead quality is sliding. Which pattern is this?
options: The ceiling account
The slow-rot account
The over-reliant account
The saturation account
questions.explain: The slow-rot account: surface metrics look healthy while lead quality quietly degrades. It usually traces back to a data/pixel-quality problem, not creative — which is why the audit checks pixel health, not just the ads.

questions.prompt: An account has tested 14 distinct angles in the last 30 days and has three clear winners, but CPA climbs every time you push past $3K/day. All the traffic goes to one book-a-call funnel. Which play does it need next?
options: Play 1: more, better ads — 14 angles still isn't enough
Play 2: a better funnel for cold traffic — the creative is working, so the funnel is the ceiling
Play 3: add a new platform to find fresh audiences
Hold spend where CPA is acceptable and let the winners mature
questions.explain: Play 1 is genuinely finished here — 14 angles with three winners clears the 10+ bar. When the creative is working and CPA still climbs with spend, the ceiling is the funnel, not the ads, so it's Play 2. Play 3 only comes once the funnel can absorb the traffic, and holding spend just accepts the ceiling.

questions.prompt: Your cost-per-call target is $300. An ad set has spent $620 with zero calls and normal-looking click costs. Per kill criteria, what do you do?
options: Keep going — it hasn't reached 3× KPI (~$900) yet
Cut it now — $620 with no calls is already a loser
Cut it — any ad set with zero calls should be killed immediately
Double its budget to force a conversion
questions.explain: 3× KPI on a $300 target is ~$900. At $620 with normal click costs you don't have enough data yet — keep going. You'd only cut earlier if a leading indicator (e.g. click cost 2–3× normal) was screaming on day one.

questions.prompt: On a conversion campaign meant to find $150k+ earners, you spot a CPM about a third of your usual. Why is that usually a warning sign, not a win?
options: A low-quality placement or audience pocket (often FB Reels) is winning the cheap auctions — that traffic won't convert
It means your creative is finally efficient, so you should scale it hard
Meta lowered ad prices that week, so enjoy it
Low CPM is always good — there's nothing to investigate
questions.explain: CPM tracks audience quality. A suspiciously cheap CPM usually means you've drifted into a low-value placement/pocket (FB Reels, Audience Network) whose cheap clicks won't convert. Investigate the cheap traffic — don't celebrate it.

questions.prompt: An ad has a 2% CTR, a 35% hook rate, and a gorgeous thumb-stop ratio — but it hasn't produced a single sale. What's the AdClass call?
options: Scale it — those metrics mean sales will come
Keep it running at low budget for the social proof
Kill it — engagement isn't the right attention, and the wrong people clicking is worse than no one
Duplicate it into a CBO to find a better pocket
questions.explain: The vanity-metrics trap: engagement shows the ad got attention, not the right attention. The wrong people clicking burns budget and feeds Meta bad signal about who to find. Great surface metrics + zero conversions = kill it.

questions.prompt: Select all the signs that point to a STARVED pixel (rather than a creative problem).
options: Only 1–3 of your optimization event show in Events Manager over the last 7 days
Link CTR is steady or improving, but the qualified-lead % is sliding
The sales team says the leads are getting worse
CPM is suddenly 3× higher than your normal
The ad has lots of likes and shares
questions.explain: A starved pixel = too few optimization events for Meta to learn from, so it optimizes for who'll engage, not who'll convert (clicks fine, quality rotting). First fix: confirm the event is actually firing (CAPI/automation) — don't change creative or budget yet.

questions.prompt: Your pod leader assigns you a live account and you run the full 7-step audit framework. What are you expected to hand in?
options: A diagnosis — which stuck-account pattern it is and which play it needs — with no changes proposed yet
A complete list of changes to implement in the account immediately
A fresh batch of creative to launch today
A scaling plan to take it to $50K/day
questions.explain: The audit stops at diagnosis only: name the pattern, name the play, flag 1–2 leading-indicator risks. Proposing and making changes comes later. The whole point is diagnose before you fix.

questions.prompt: A teammate wants to spend the whole week perfecting campaign structure to fix an account's flat results. Per AdClass's core belief, is that the highest-leverage use of their time?
options: Yes — structure is the main driver of results
No — structure is only ~10–20% of results; creative and offer drive 80–90%
Yes — structure and bidding together are about half of results
No — audience targeting settings are what matter most
questions.explain: Structure is only ~10–20% of results. The leverage is in creative and offer (80–90%). Reorganizing the account rarely fixes flat performance.

questions.prompt: Your PMA flags that a campaign they built is underperforming and asks whether to restructure it. Who makes that call, and what do you owe them?
options: They do — they built it, so it's their call
Escalate it to Matthew
You do — the strategic decision is yours. They bring options and a recommendation, you decide, and you tell them why
Split it — they decide structure, you decide creative
questions.explain: The PMA owns execution; the PMS owns the strategic decision and the outcome. The half people miss is telling them why — that's what makes it a decision they learn from rather than an override. Nothing here needs Matthew.

questions.prompt: You've diagnosed a slow-rot (pixel/data) problem an account has had for weeks. First move with the client?
options: Say nothing until it's fixed
Wait for them to raise it on the weekly call
Proactively flag it with the cause, the fix, and a timeline — before they feel the lead-quality drop
Tell the sales team it's their problem
questions.explain: Proactivity plus honest-with-a-plan. A client who discovers a weeks-old data problem themselves has learned something worse than the problem: that you knew and didn't say.

4.title: Day 4 — Funnel Auditing
4.sub: The landing page as a targeting signal; finding the drop-off. ~10 min.

questions.prompt: Two ads are identical — same copy, same pixel — but one points to a masculine-designed funnel and the other to a feminine-designed one. What happens to delivery?
options: Nothing — the landing page doesn't affect ad delivery
Meta serves them to different audiences — it reads the page's copy and design as a targeting signal
Meta rejects the feminine-designed one
Delivery is identical because the pixel is the same
questions.explain: Meta scans your landing page — bounce rate, time on page, copy, even the design's feel — and uses it as a targeting signal. The page is part of the ad system, not downstream of it. Same ad, different page = different audience.

questions.prompt: A lead magnet has run two weeks at about the same cost-per-lead as the application funnel. The team wants to kill it. What's the AdClass view?
options: Kill it — same CPL means it isn't working
Keep it — judge a lead magnet on pipeline contribution at ~day 60, not direct revenue at day 14
Double the budget immediately
Convert it into a low-ticket funnel
questions.explain: The lead magnet's job is firing qualified pixel events at scale, building a database for SDR follow-up, and seeding a 30–60 day nurture. Judge it on pipeline at day 60, not CPL or revenue at day 14.

questions.prompt: Your audit shows the landing page converting clicks to opt-ins at 9% — the weakest step in the funnel. You have messaging, design and page structure to work with. What do you do?
options: Rebuild all three at once to have it ready before the client call
Change one at a time so you can tell which one moved it, starting with messaging
Raise the budget to gather more data before touching anything
Change the audience so better-qualified traffic hits the page
questions.explain: One lever at a time, or you get a result and no idea what caused it. Messaging first because it's the heaviest of the three. And a page problem doesn't get solved by buying more traffic for it — that's paying more to lose at the same rate.

questions.prompt: More than 60% of traffic is mobile. Select all the checks that belong on a mobile-view funnel audit.
options: Does the opt-in form actually work on mobile?
Does the video autoplay / play correctly?
Is anything visually broken or cut off on a phone?
Does the page load fast enough (no long delay)?
What's the desktop hero image's resolution?
What's the campaign's CBO-vs-ABO setting?
questions.explain: Most of your traffic experiences the funnel on a phone, so check the form works, the video autoplays, nothing's broken, and the page loads fast. Desktop image resolution and the campaign's budget setting aren't part of a mobile funnel audit.

questions.prompt: A client is hitting a frequency ceiling on their single book-a-call funnel and can't scale. What funnel-layer fix does AdClass recommend?
options: Just raise the budget on the existing funnel
Narrow the audience targeting
Run multiple funnels hitting different audience stages (e.g. TOF lead magnet + MOF VSL + BOF retargeting), each with its own optimization event
Lower the bid cap
questions.explain: A single funnel optimized for one event taps out one pocket — frequency climbs and costs rise. Running different funnels at different stages (different optimization events) opens pockets the others can't reach. Multiple offers/pages are the new multiple ads.

questions.prompt: Your funnel audit has to end with 3 specific observations. Which one is acceptable, AdClass-style?
options: “The page could be better.”
“H1 says 'blueprint' but the ads say 'system' — change the H1 to match the ad.”
“Make the whole funnel nicer.”
“Add more colors and testimonials everywhere.”
questions.explain: Observations must be specific and actionable — name the exact problem and the fix. Vague notes like “could be better” aren't usable on a client call.

questions.prompt: An account's CTR is steady and CPL is flat, but the qualified-lead % has been sliding for months. Where do you look first?
options: Data/pixel quality — is the optimization event firing reliably and at enough volume?
The headline font color
The CBO budget split
The length of the ad copy
questions.explain: Healthy clicks + rotting quality is the classic starved/again mis-firing pixel pattern. If Meta isn't getting a clean conversion signal, it optimizes for who will engage, not who will convert. Audit the firing first.

questions.prompt: A client sells a $47 ebook with an order bump and has no sales team. Which funnel are you building, and what does that change about the optimisation event?
options: VSL funnel — optimise for Schedule
Lead-magnet funnel — optimise for Lead
Webinar funnel — optimise for Registration
Low-ticket funnel — optimise for Purchase, since the sale completes on-site
questions.explain: No call means no Schedule event to optimise toward, and the purchase completes inside the funnel — so Purchase is both available and the furthest-along event. The funnel type and the optimisation event are the same decision, made once.

5.title: Day 5 — Creative Philosophy
5.sub: Hooks, angles, the anatomy matrix, and coaching creative work. ~10 min.

questions.prompt: What's the difference between Pillar 1 (Creative Diversity) and Pillar 2 (Angle Testing)?
options: Pillar 1 floods volume and variety of creative to discover pockets; Pillar 2 isolates which messaging/angle actually resonates
Pillar 1 is about budget; Pillar 2 is about bidding
They're two names for the same thing
Pillar 1 is scaling winners; Pillar 2 is killing losers
questions.explain: Pillar 1 (Creative Diversity) is the foundation — high volume/variety so the algorithm discovers audience pockets. Pillar 2 (Angle Testing) is the discovery engine — finding the hook/messaging that resonates. Pillar 3 scales the winners.

questions.prompt: Why call out an identity (“Dallas executives”) rather than an objection (“or you don't pay”)?
options: Identity callouts attract people already half-sold the offer is for them; objection/guarantee callouts attract skeptics who convert poorly
Objection callouts are banned by Meta
Identity callouts are just cheaper per click
There's no real difference
questions.explain: People who self-identify with your ad are the people who click and convert. Guarantee/objection headlines pull in skeptics who came in worried about their money. Call out the identity you want in the buyer, not the objection you want to defuse.

questions.prompt: You launch an ad set testing a new hook, a new image, AND new targeting all at once. The winner pops. What did you actually learn?
options: Nothing reliable — you changed multiple variables, so you can't attribute the result
That the new image caused the win
That the new targeting caused the win
Everything — it was a perfect test
questions.explain: A valid test isolates one variable (hook, format, CTA, visual, or avatar) and holds everything else constant. “If you're testing everything, you're testing nothing.”

questions.prompt: What's one rule for scaling info / high-ticket creative?
options: Always move winners into a fresh CBO immediately
Scale in place — don't disturb a working ad set by dropping new post-IDs into it
Use cost caps on book-a-call campaigns
Add 200% daily budget jumps
questions.explain: For info/high-ticket, scale in place. Dropping a new post-ID into a scaled ad set makes Meta re-hunt a pocket and spikes call-cost volatility. Cost caps are for high-volume low-ticket/purchase, not low-volume book-a-call.

questions.prompt: One angle is working — "stop guessing what your ads should say." You need a dozen new concepts from it this week without changing the angle. What do you vary?
options: Camera style, ad format, filming trend and editing trend — the same angle rebuilt several ways along each axis
The audience and the placements
The hook only, keeping everything else identical
The offer, to see which version converts best
questions.explain: That's the ad anatomy matrix: the angle is the constant, the axes are the variables. Varying the offer changes what you're testing entirely. Audience and placements aren't creative variables. Hook-only gets you a handful of near-identical ads, not a dozen distinct concepts.

questions.prompt: When should you judge a lead magnet — and on what?
options: Day 14, on cost-per-lead vs. the application funnel
Day 60, on its pipeline contribution
Day 7, on direct ROAS
Day 30, on immediate revenue
questions.explain: Judge a lead magnet on pipeline contribution at ~day 60, not direct revenue/CPL at day 14. Its job is qualified pixel events, list-building, and seeding nurture.

questions.prompt: A PMA's script opens with 30 seconds of brand backstory before any hook. Reviewing it as PMS, what's your note?
options: It's fine — backstory builds trust
Add pricing earlier
Make it longer
Lead with the hook (0–5s) — pattern interrupt / claim / curiosity — then problem, mechanism, CTA
questions.explain: The first five seconds decide whether the rest gets watched. Backstory can earn trust after attention exists, never before it.

6.title: Day 6 — Competitor Research
6.sub: Ad Library work, angle gaps, SWOT. ~10 min.

questions.prompt: In the Meta Ad Library, what's the quickest tell that a competitor's ad is probably a winner?
options: It's been running 30+ days
It has the most likes and comments
It uses the most colors
It's their newest ad
questions.explain: Longevity is the first signal — an ad live 30+ days is almost certainly working for them. Second check: a traffic-ranker (SimilarWeb-style) to confirm the page actually gets meaningful traffic before you model their strategy.

questions.prompt: Every competitor in the niche is running "make $10K/month" income claims. Your client's buyers keep saying on sales calls that what they're sick of is the hours, not the money. What have you found?
options: A weakness in your client's offer
A reason to match the competitors' income claims more aggressively
A targeting problem — you're reaching the wrong buyers
An angle gap — a callout the whole market is ignoring that your client could own
questions.explain: An angle gap is a callout nobody is running that your buyers are already saying out loud. The tell is exactly this: a mismatch between what the market advertises and what the calls reveal. Matching everyone else's claim is how you compete on the crowded axis instead of the empty one.

questions.prompt: Why is cloning a competitor's winning ads usually a mistake?
options: You want the angles they're NOT running (gaps you can own); remix proven hooks rather than clone them
Cloning ads is illegal
Their ads never actually work
Meta bans duplicate creative
questions.explain: Clone and you're fighting on their turf, usually with less brand equity. Use the Ad Library to find gaps to own, and remix proven hooks rather than copying ads outright.

questions.prompt: AdClass narrows a market base → subcategory → niche → super-niche. Why go as tight as possible?
options: It makes the targetable audience bigger
The tighter the super-niche, the sharper your competitor list and angle gaps
It automatically lowers CPMs
Meta requires a declared super-niche
questions.explain: A tighter super-niche gives a sharper competitor set and sharper angle gaps. Also sanity-check targetability (can it even run on Meta/Google?) and market size (too small can't scale, too broad won't bite).

questions.prompt: In a performance SWOT you write down: "no competitor is speaking to buyers over 45, and the client's strongest testimonials skew that way." Which quadrant does that belong in?
options: Strength
Weakness
Opportunity
Threat
questions.explain: It's external and unclaimed — an audience pocket nobody is talking to, which is what Opportunities captures. Strengths are the client's own advantages; the testimonials are a strength, but the finding here is the gap in the market. It only becomes a threat once a competitor moves on it.

questions.prompt: A much bigger competitor is rumored to be entering your client's market. In a performance SWOT, that's a…
options: Strength
Weakness
Opportunity
Threat
questions.explain: Threat = what could erode the account fast (a bigger competitor entering, a platform change, seasonality). Strength = the client's unfair advantage; Weakness = where prospects bounce; Opportunity = angle gaps / untapped pockets.

questions.prompt: Beyond studying a competitor's ads, what else does AdClass tell you to do in competitor research?
options: Walk their actual funnel — offer, price point, page structure — often more telling than the creative
Copy their top ad word-for-word
Report their ads to Meta
Nothing — only the ads matter
questions.explain: From the ad's “Learn more,” walk the whole funnel: the offer, price point (low-ticket checkout vs. high-ticket VSL + call), and page structure. It's often more instructive than the creative itself.

questions.prompt: When testing angles, you group ad sets by ___.
options: Format
Angle
Audience
Placement
questions.explain: Group by angle, mixing formats inside each angle. The angle is the thesis; format variety is how Meta finds the right person for it.

questions.prompt: Does the landing page affect which audience Meta shows your ad to?
options: No — only the ad creative and pixel matter
Yes — Meta reads the page, so it's a targeting signal
Only on desktop
Only if you change the pixel
questions.explain: Yes — the landing page is a targeting signal. Meta reads the copy and design and serves accordingly; even a one-word headline change can shift who sees the ad.

7.title: Day 7 — Data Review
7.sub: Reading an account honestly; which numbers actually decide things. ~10 min.

questions.prompt: Why look at 7-, 14-, AND 30-day windows every time before you cut, scale, or change something?
options: 7-day = what's happening now, 14-day = the recent trend, 30-day = the baseline; if 7 disagrees with 30 you have a question, not a decision
To make the report look longer
Because Meta requires all three
Only the 7-day actually matters
questions.explain: Each window answers a different question. When the 7-day disagrees with the 30-day you don't yet have a decision — especially on high-ticket, where sales cycles run longer than you think.

questions.prompt: Select all of the following that are LEADING indicators (they move within 1–3 days).
options: CPM
Link CTR
CPC
Hook rate (3-sec views)
Cost per call
ROAS
Close rate
questions.explain: Leading (1–3 days): CPM, CTR, CPC, hook rate, scroll-stop. Lagging (7–30 days): CPL, cost per call/application, ROAS, show rate, close rate. For call clients, CPC is often the single most important leading number.

questions.prompt: On a conversion campaign meant to reach $150K+ earners, your CPM is suddenly a third of normal (~$13). Warning or win?
options: Warning — a suspiciously low CPM usually means a low-quality placement/pocket whose cheap clicks won't convert
Win — cheap reach, scale it hard
Neutral — CPM doesn't mean anything
It just means the pixel broke
questions.explain: CPM tracks audience quality. A cheap CPM on a high-value conversion campaign usually means you've drifted into a low-quality placement (often FB Reels) or pocket. Investigate the cheap traffic — don't celebrate it.

questions.prompt: An ad has a 2% CTR, 35% hook rate, and a beautiful thumb-stop — and zero sales. What do you do?
options: Scale it — the metrics say sales are coming
Kill it — engagement is attention, not the right attention; the wrong people clicking is worse than no one
Keep it at low budget for the social proof
Lower the budget and wait a month
questions.explain: The vanity-metrics trap. Great engagement + zero conversions means the wrong people are clicking — burning budget and feeding Meta bad signal. Kill it.

questions.prompt: You launched 4 new ads yesterday. Day-1 CPC is 2–3× your normal. Do you wait for the full 3× KPI spend, or pull?
options: Pull — when leading indicators are badly off on day 1, you don't need to wait for full 3× KPI spend
Wait the full 3× KPI no matter what
Double the budget to gather data faster
Switch the optimization event immediately
questions.explain: When leading indicators are clearly bad on day one (CPC 2–3× normal), the creative isn't resonating — cut faster than the 3× KPI guideline. That guideline is for ambiguous cases, not obvious losers.

questions.prompt: You find a competitor ad that's been running 90 days and rebuild it almost shot for shot for your client. Why does this usually underperform?
options: Meta suppresses creative that closely resembles another advertiser's
You copied the execution without knowing which part was working, or what their offer and funnel do after the click
Ads running that long are always near the end of their life
It doesn't — cloning proven winners is the fastest route to a winner
questions.explain: A long-running ad tells you an angle works for their offer, audience and funnel. Cloning the execution copies the surface and inherits none of that. Take the angle, then rebuild it for your client's offer and the page it points at.

questions.prompt: Which converts better to call out in a headline?
options: The objection / guarantee (“or you don't pay”)
The buyer's identity (“Dallas executives”)
Neither matters
Always the lowest price
questions.explain: Call out the identity you want in the buyer. Identity callouts attract people already half-sold; objection/guarantee callouts attract skeptics who convert poorly.

questions.prompt: A client sells a $9K program to “business owners.” You want to narrow the callout to “HVAC owners doing $2–5M.” They're worried about shrinking the audience. What's the argument?
options: Meta rewards smaller audiences with cheaper delivery
A tighter callout makes the ad unmistakably for them, which lifts CTR and lead quality — and you can run several niches in parallel instead of one vague ad
Broad audiences stopped working on Meta
It doesn't matter much — the algorithm finds the right people either way
questions.explain: We narrow base → subcategory → niche → super-niche because specificity earns the click. “Business owners” speaks to nobody; “HVAC owners doing $2–5M” speaks to somebody. Audience size isn't the constraint, because every niche that works opens another pocket.

8.title: Day 8 — AI Foundations at AdClass
8.sub: How AdClass uses AI; the tools, the guardrails, the client-data line. ~10 min.

questions.prompt: What's AdClass's core principle about how it uses AI?
options: AI is a replacement for media buyers
AI is leverage — do more of the work that compounds, less of the work that doesn't (manual entry, reformatting)
AI is only useful for writing copy
AI is a toy, not for real client work
questions.explain: AI is leverage, not replacement. Use it to do more of the compounding work (creative iteration, data analysis, audit speed) and less of the busywork that doesn't move the needle.

questions.prompt: Select all the places AI actually shows up in a PMS's day at AdClass.
options: Generating new creative angle variants from winning ad transcripts + LP context
Accelerating audits — finding anomalies in a PPC sheet
Drafting creative briefs from intake + competitor research
Meeting prep — Fathom transcript + Notion + Slack into a cited doc
Auto-approving client invoices
Setting the client's pricing for them
questions.explain: Everyday PMS uses: creative iteration (transcripts + LP → new angles), audit acceleration, brief writing, and meeting prep. It speeds the work; it doesn't make business decisions like pricing or approvals.

questions.prompt: Why run human-voice-copy AFTER the other copy skills, not before?
options: It's the final pass that strips AI tells out of finished copy — run it first and the other skills just re-introduce them
It generates the first draft for the other skills to edit
It only works on images
Order doesn't matter
questions.explain: human-voice-copy is the final filter. It makes already-written copy sound human, so it has to run last — otherwise the generation skills add the robotic tells right back.

questions.prompt: You ask Claude to pull the top objections out of 40 client sales-call transcripts and it returns a clean, confident list. Working fluently with it means doing what next?
options: Trusting it — speed is the whole point of using it
Spot-checking the output against a few real transcripts before any of it reaches the client
Re-running the same prompt until two answers agree
Rewriting the list in your own words so it doesn't sound like AI
questions.explain: AI Fluency is collaborating with these systems effectively, efficiently, ethically and safely — and the discernment half is what stops confident-and-wrong output reaching a client. Re-running a prompt tests consistency, not accuracy. Rewording changes the voice, not whether it's true.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a leading indicator (moves within 1–3 days)?
options: Cost per call
CTR / CPC / hook rate
ROAS
Close rate
questions.explain: Leading (1–3 days): CPM, CTR, CPC, hook rate, scroll-stop. Lagging (7–30 days): CPL, cost per call, ROAS, close rate.

questions.prompt: What's an “angle gap”?
options: A gap in your ad scheduling
A callout/hook/angle competitors aren't running that your client could own
The difference between two bid amounts
A missing pixel event
questions.explain: An angle gap is an angle the market isn't running that your client can claim — the whole point of competitor research.

questions.prompt: A PMA wants to paste a client's raw call recordings into a consumer AI tool to speed up angle research. As PMS, what do you do?
options: Let it go — speed matters most
Stop it — use approved tools/skills and keep client data out of unvetted tools; then show the sanctioned workflow
Do it yourself the same way
Ban all AI use
questions.explain: Two things at once: hold the client-data line, and then show the sanctioned workflow — because a stop with no replacement just gets worked around quietly next time. Banning AI outright throws away the leverage.

10.title: Day 10 — Media Buying I: Campaign Launches & Optimizations
10.sub: Structure, launch decisions, and the first two weeks of an account. ~10 min.

questions.prompt: An e-commerce client with high purchase volume — ABO or CBO for scaling winners?
options: ABO — always control budget manually
CBO — post-ID winners into a CBO works well for e-com/low-ticket with high conversion volume
Neither — only use Advantage+ Shopping
It doesn't matter
questions.explain: CBO. With high conversion volume (e-com/low-ticket), post-ID winners into a CBO lets Meta allocate budget across proven concepts and preserves social proof. ABO stays the default for low-volume info/high-ticket where you want manual pacing.

questions.prompt: On a call funnel you'd normally optimize for Schedule. When would you optimize for Lead instead?
options: When you're deliberately running a top-of-funnel list-building play (or Schedule volume is too low to optimize on)
Never — always optimize for Schedule
Whenever the client says they want more leads
Whenever CPM looks low
questions.explain: Default is the furthest-along event you can get volume on (Schedule). Drop to Lead when you're intentionally building a TOF list — or step up the funnel temporarily when the Schedule event is too starved for Meta to optimize on.

questions.prompt: Your client's page posts about fitness, but the offer is a business-coaching program — Advantage+ keeps hammering the warm fitness audience. What's the fix?
options: Raise the budget on the main campaign
Switch the campaign to exact-match keywords
Run a dedicated low-budget cold-prospecting ad set, excluding page engagers, ad engagers, video viewers, and website visitors
Delete the Facebook page
questions.explain: That's page incongruence: the page's signals don't match the offer, so Advantage+ pulls the wrong warm audience. Fix with a low-budget ($100–200/day) cold-prospecting ad set excluding warm engagers for ~180 days (the Local Legend example).

questions.prompt: Why exclude past purchasers and booked calls even when you're on Advantage+ broad?
options: Because past purchasers cost more to reach
Exclusions are guardrails — they stop Meta recycling your existing pipeline instead of finding new people
Because Meta requires the exclusion
Because it lowers your CPM
questions.explain: Exclusions aren't targeting inputs — they're guardrails. They keep Advantage+ from re-serving people already in your pipeline so your prospecting budget actually finds new audiences.

questions.prompt: Select all that match AdClass's default audience approach.
options: Advantage+ broad is the default
Interests and lookalikes work as seed audiences layered in, not hard constraints
Exclude past purchasers / booked calls to keep prospecting cold
Always build tight interest stacks as hard targeting
Never use exclusions of any kind
questions.explain: Advantage+ broad is the default; interests/lookalikes are seeds layered in (not hard constraints); exclusions are guardrails. Tight hard-interest stacks and “never exclude” are both the old playbook.

questions.prompt: A $12K coaching offer has one ad set producing calls at target. Your PMA wants to drop three new winning post-IDs into that ad set to scale faster. What do you tell them?
options: Go ahead — more winners inside a working ad set compounds
Leave the working ad set alone. Raise its budget 20–40% and duplicate for the new creative, so you don't disturb what's already delivering
Move everything into a CBO with cost caps
Launch the three new post-IDs and pause the current winner to free the budget
questions.explain: For info and high-ticket, scale in place. Dropping new post-IDs into a scaled ad set disturbs Meta's distribution and call costs turn volatile — a $100 → $300 swing in a day isn't unusual on a low-volume call funnel. Post-ID migration into a CBO is an e-com / high-purchase-volume move.

questions.prompt: The 7-day window says an ad set is your best performer. The 30-day window says it's your worst. What do you do?
options: Trust the 7-day — it's the most recent signal
Trust the 30-day — more data is more reliable
Neither yet. You don't have a decision, you have a question — find out what changed between the windows first
Average the two and decide from that
questions.explain: You check 7, 14 and 30 every time precisely so disagreements surface. When the windows disagree, something changed — new creative, an audience shift, a tracking break. Find the change first. Acting on one window alone is how you kill a recovering ad set or scale a dying one.

questions.prompt: For an info/high-ticket book-a-call client protecting a proven winner, which do you lean toward and why?
options: CBO — it's always cheaper
Neither — only Advantage+ Shopping
ABO — control budget at the ad-set level so you can scale in place without disturbing the winner
It never matters
questions.explain: ABO keeps the budget decision at the ad-set level, so a proven winner can be scaled without the campaign redistributing spend away from it. 'Always cheaper' is not a property either option has.

questions.prompt: You changed the optimization event 4 days ago and performance looks worse. Do you revert?
options: No — pixel changes take ~14 days to recalibrate; reverting at day 4 means you'll never know if it worked
Yes, revert immediately
Yes, and change three other things while you're at it
Double the budget to speed it up
questions.explain: The 14-day rule: Meta re-trains over ~14 days after any pixel/optimization/exclusion change. Panic-reverting at day 4 is how accounts stay broken for months.

questions.prompt: To test a new creative or audience, what do you do — and what do you never do?
options: Edit the live ad set directly to save time
Duplicate the ad set (or launch a new one) — never drop the change into a live, working ad set
Delete the ad set and rebuild it from scratch
Pause the whole campaign first
questions.explain: Golden rule: never modify a live ad set. Adding into it muddies data, steals delivery from what's working, and resets learning. Duplicate instead. (OK in place: budget/bid, pausing losers.)

questions.prompt: When is it OK to cut an ad set BEFORE it hits 3× KPI spend?
options: Never — always wait for the full 3× KPI
When day-1 click cost is 2–3× your normal (or a diversity-play static has an absurd CPC)
When the ad has fewer than 100 likes
When the client asks you to
questions.explain: Cut faster when leading indicators are obviously bad on day one (CPC 2–3× normal), or on diversity-play statics with absurd CPCs — you don't need conversion data to know it's a loser.

questions.prompt: Select all the things you check on the daily optimization pass.
options: Verify the VA's reported numbers, then confirm against Hyros
Run a 7 / 14 / 30-day comparison on the key metrics
What's eating budget (top spender) and what's converting
Anything past 3× KPI without a conversion (kill candidates)
The 20% net-new test budget — has anything emerged?
Redesign the landing page from scratch
Rewrite all the ad copy
questions.explain: The daily OS: verify the VA's numbers (confirm in Hyros), 7/14/30 comparison, what's eating budget, what's converting, what's past kill criteria, what's net-new, and the leading-indicator picture. Redesigning pages or rewriting all copy isn't a daily task.

questions.prompt: For a book-a-call client, you check the booking calendar every morning. Why?
options: To count the client's revenue
To pace spend to availability — don't pay to book an already-full calendar; scale when there are open slots
To schedule your own calls
It's not actually necessary
questions.explain: Pace spend to the calendar: few open slots → ease off (don't pay to fill a booked calendar); lots of openings → room to scale. Rough math: open slots × cost-per-call = spend needed.

questions.prompt: A PMA sends you ad copy that reads well but is unmistakably AI — tidy, rhythmic, a little lifeless. They ran human-voice-copy first, then drm-ad-copy. What went wrong?
options: Nothing — that's just how AI copy reads
The order. human-voice-copy is the final pass, so running it first means the generation skill puts the tells straight back in
They should have used human-voice-copy on its own
They needed to run it three or four times
questions.explain: human-voice-copy is a filter, not a generator. It strips AI tells out of finished copy, so it runs last. Run it first and whatever writes the copy afterwards re-introduces everything it just removed.

12.title: Day 12 — Google Ads: Search Campaigns
12.sub: Intent, match types, and where Search fits alongside Meta. ~8 min.

questions.prompt: What's the difference between brand and non-brand search — and which one scales?
options: Brand targets the client's own name (cheap, high-intent, low volume); non-brand targets general terms and is what scales
Non-brand targets the brand name; brand is what scales
They're the same thing
Brand search scales infinitely
questions.explain: Brand = the client's own name/products — cheap, sky-high intent, but low volume (doesn't scale). Non-brand = general terms — scalable and broad, but needs tighter control to keep quality up.

questions.prompt: Which two networks do you turn OFF at setup, and why?
options: YouTube + Gmail — they cost too much
Search Partners + Display Network — the single biggest bot-traffic lever
Search + Shopping — they don't convert
None — leave everything on
questions.explain: Turn OFF Search Partners + Display Network at setup — it's the single biggest lever against bot traffic. Confirm it stuck after launch.

questions.prompt: Select all the levers AdClass uses to fight bot traffic on Google Search.
options: Deselect “Unknown” for age, gender, and household income
Exclude all non-US countries in bulk
Keep Search Partners + Display Network turned off
Switch the campaign to Performance Max
Turn the Display Network on
Raise the daily budget
questions.explain: Bot prevention is the whole game on Google: deselect “Unknown” demographics, bulk-exclude non-US countries (Nigeria/India/China are common culprits), and keep Search Partners + Display off. Performance Max and Display are bot magnets — not levers against bots.

questions.prompt: How can a Search campaign optimize for lead quality, not just lead volume?
options: Add a Purchase conversion fired via Hyros CAPI, so Google chases higher-quality leads while still optimizing the easy event
Just raise the daily budget
Switch all keywords to Broad match
Turn on Performance Max
questions.explain: Use a campaign-specific conversion goal and also add Purchase via Hyros CAPI — Google then chases higher-quality leads while still optimizing the easy event (Lead/Call).

questions.prompt: Why doesn't AdClass use Performance Max?
options: It's too expensive to enable
Google's AI decides everything — cheap leads sometimes, but near-impossible to optimize
It only works for Meta
It's banned for agencies
questions.explain: Performance Max hands all control to Google's AI — occasionally cheap leads, but you can't steer it. AdClass also disables Display (bot magnet) and ignores Shopping (e-com only).

questions.prompt: For a book-a-call funnel, what's the default optimization event?
options: Lead
Schedule / booked call
Purchase
Landing page view
questions.explain: Optimize for the furthest-along event you can get volume on — on a call funnel that's Schedule. (Same logic applies when you set Google's conversion goal.)

17.title: Day 17 — Leadership I: Trust, Coaching & Leading People Well
17.sub: Questions 1–14 plus three from Section E. Scenario-based — pick the response you'd actually give. ~15 min.

questions.prompt: Your PMA tells you, in confidence, that they think another pod's PMS is cutting corners on a client's reporting. They ask you not to say anything. What's the best response?
options: Keep it in confidence — they trusted you, and breaking that would end the trust.
Go to Matthew yourself, without telling your PMA, so they aren't implicated.
Tell them you can't promise confidentiality on something like this, and that the right move is for them to raise it with that PMS directly, with your help preparing for it.
Look into the other pod's reporting quietly yourself before deciding anything.
questions.explain: Two principles collide here: don't talk about people behind their back, and don't accept a confidence you can't keep. The move is to renegotiate the confidentiality before you hear more, then coach them to raise it themselves — with your help preparing. Promising silence makes you complicit; going over their head silently teaches them that telling you things has unpredictable consequences.

questions.prompt: A PMA on another pod messages you: "Is it just me or does [their PMS] not actually know what they're doing?" You privately think they have a point. Best response?
options: "That's a real thing to raise, but I'm the wrong person. What have you said to them directly?"
"I've noticed some of that too — but you should talk to them about it."
Don't respond, and mention it to their PMS later.
"I can't get into that, sorry."
questions.explain: Take the concern seriously and redirect it to the only person who can fix it. Validating the criticism to a third party is participating in it, however constructive it sounds — and it will get quoted. Shutting the door entirely is safe but closes off a real problem.

questions.prompt: You made a bad strategic call two weeks ago. Your PMA flagged the risk at the time and you overruled them. The account is now down and a client call is tomorrow. What do you do first?
options: Build the recovery plan, then tell your PMA on the call tomorrow so you have a solution to present.
Focus forward — relitigating it now just undermines your authority when you need to look decisive.
Tell Matthew first, then decide what to say to your PMA.
Tell your PMA today that they were right, that you got it wrong, and build the recovery plan with them.
questions.explain: This is the vulnerability-based trust question, and what you're buying is the next time your PMA sees a risk. Unacknowledged errors don't protect authority — they cost you the next warning. Matthew does need to know, but your PMA is the one owed it first, and finding out on a client call means finding out publicly.

questions.prompt: Your pod has been in complete agreement on everything for two months. Nothing is on fire. Is anything wrong?
options: No — that's a well-functioning pod.
Possibly. Sustained total agreement usually means someone has stopped saying what they think.
No, but you should introduce disagreement exercises to keep things sharp.
Yes — it means your PMA isn't being challenged enough and needs harder work.
questions.explain: Artificial harmony is the more expensive option. Note the answer is possibly, not definitely — the right instinct is curiosity, not alarm, and conflict is not a target to hit.

questions.prompt: Your PMA's last four weekly reports each had a small but different error. Individually trivial. What's the most useful thing to address?
options: Each error, so they know exactly what was wrong in each case.
Put a QA checklist in place and don't make it a conversation.
The fact that there were four — the pattern of not self-checking before sending, not the four items.
Nothing yet; they're small and the PMA is new.
questions.explain: Cataloguing four corrections teaches nothing and leaves them feeling incompetent. The pattern is the lesson. A checklist alongside the conversation is arguably ideal; a checklist instead of it means the problem returns the moment the checklist gets boring.

questions.prompt: On a pod call with three other people, your PMA states a number that you know is wrong. What do you do in the moment?
options: Say the number needs a second look before anyone acts on it, without assigning it to them, then handle it with them privately after.
Correct it immediately and move on — accuracy matters more than comfort.
Say nothing on the call and correct it in the follow-up notes.
Ask them on the call to double-check where the number came from.
questions.explain: Praise in public, critique in private — under time pressure. Accuracy is non-negotiable and the correction doesn't have to be attributed. If you think you have to choose between the two, look again.

questions.prompt: You've asked your PMA three times to change how they name campaigns. It keeps happening. Most likely explanation, and best next move?
options: They're careless — escalate to a formal conversation about attention to detail.
They don't care about the convention — explain why it matters again, more forcefully.
Do it yourself going forward; it's faster than the third conversation.
Something in how they work makes the correct way harder than the wrong way — sit with them while they do it once and find out what.
questions.explain: By the third repetition, 'they're careless' has been disproven — you've told them twice, so a third telling, louder, predicts nothing different. Ask before you tell, applied to a discipline problem rather than a knowledge problem. Doing it yourself makes you the permanent bottleneck.

questions.prompt: Your PMA did excellent work on a competitor analysis that you then presented to a client, who loved it. What's the highest-value thing you can do?
options: Tell your PMA privately that the client loved it.
Mention it in their next 1:1 as evidence they're progressing.
Tell the client it was your PMA's work, and tell your PMA in a channel where the people whose opinion they care about will see it.
Thank them and give them the next competitor analysis to own outright.
questions.explain: Public credit is free and asymmetric. The 'in front of the people whose opinion they care about' detail is the 1% lens, and it's what separates a strong answer from a fine one. A 1:1 mention weeks later isn't praise, it's record-keeping — and stacking more work on good work with no recognition is how people learn to hide their capability.

questions.prompt: A PMA who is normally sharp has been quietly slower and more withdrawn for two weeks. Nothing has actually been missed. What's the best opening?
options: Wait — nothing's broken, and prying is worse than patience.
"You've seemed a bit off lately and I wanted to check in. No agenda — is everything alright?"
"Your output's been slower the last couple of weeks — what's going on?"
Reduce their workload quietly to give them room.
questions.explain: Nothing has been missed — so this isn't a performance conversation, and opening it as one is the error. A performance framing on a human signal makes an anxious person defensive. Quietly cutting their workload solves a problem you haven't diagnosed and reads as being demoted.

questions.prompt: You need to give your PMA critical feedback, and you know they take it hard. What's the best framing?
options: Name the standard, be specific about the one behaviour, and be explicit that your confidence in them isn't in question.
Lead with several genuine positives to soften it, then deliver the criticism.
Be brief and clinical so it's over quickly.
Ask them how they think they've been doing, and hope they raise it themselves.
questions.explain: Separate the standard from the person — and say the regard part out loud. The compliment sandwich teaches people that praise from you is a warning sign, which poisons the praise. Clinical brevity protects you, not them; hoping they raise it outsources your job to their self-awareness.

questions.prompt: Your PMA has built a genuinely good relationship with a client, who now Slacks them directly with strategy questions instead of you. What's the right move?
options: Nothing — a client who trusts your PMA is a good outcome.
Ask the client to route strategy questions through you.
Loop yourself into the DMs so you can see everything.

Tell your PMA to redirect strategy questions to you, keep the relationship warm, and make sure the client knows why — that you own the strategy so they get the best answer, not because your PMA is being sidelined.
questions.explain: Three things at once: the boundary, the relationship, and the explanation. Most people get one or two. Fixing the routing without the context lands as a demotion for your PMA and a rebuff for the client; leaving it alone means they field strategy they don't own and you hear about decisions late.

questions.prompt: Your PMA hands you a first-draft audit at roughly 70% of your standard, two days before the client call. What do you do?
options: Rewrite it to your standard, send it, and give feedback after the call.
Sit with them for 30 minutes, work the biggest two gaps together, and have them finish it.
Send it back with your notes and a tight deadline, then review again.
Present it as-is and let the client's reaction be the lesson.
questions.explain: Two days is enough time. Rewriting it gets you a good deck and a PMA who learned nothing and knows you rewrote it. Notes on a page transfer far less than working it together. Worth noting: if it were two hours, rewriting becomes right — and sacrificing a client for a lesson never is.

questions.prompt: A client asks your PMA on a call whether the last test "worked." Your PMA doesn't know the answer. What should they have been trained to say?
options: Give their best read so the client doesn't lose confidence.
Defer to you in the moment.
"Let me check and come back to you today" — and then actually do.
Explain that it's too early to judge, since that's usually true.
questions.explain: "I don't know, and here's when I'll know" is a complete answer, including to a client. Inventing confidence risks a wrong answer in a client's notes. Deferring to you is fine occasionally and corrosive as a habit. And 'too early to judge' is the sneaky one — it's often true, which makes it a comfortable way to avoid admitting you don't know.

questions.prompt: Six weeks in, your PMA asks to sit in on strategy calls. They're not ready to contribute. What do you do?
options: Bring them in to listen only, with a specific thing to watch for and a debrief after.
Say not yet, and tell them what they'd need to demonstrate first.
Bring them in and let them contribute — the pressure will accelerate them.
Send them recordings instead so they can learn without the risk.
questions.explain: Show, then do. You don't have to be ready to contribute to be ready to observe — and someone asking for more exposure at six weeks is hungry, so the answer shouldn't be no. Recordings remove the thing that makes shadowing valuable, which is being in the room.

questions.prompt: Matthew gives you feedback in front of two other PMSs that you think is based on a misunderstanding of what happened. What's the best response in the room?
options: Take it, ask a clarifying question, and follow up with him privately with the fuller picture.
Correct the record immediately and politely — leaving it unchallenged lets a wrong version stand.
Say nothing at all and let it go.
Say you disagree and that you'll pick it up with him later.
questions.explain: Critique in private cuts upward too. Correcting your boss in front of peers makes the room about status rather than accuracy — right on substance, wrong on venue. Saying nothing loses the information; announcing a disagreement without resolving it leaves everyone hanging.

questions.prompt: A client complains to you, informally, that your PMA "seems junior" on calls. You think the PMA is doing fine and the client is being snobbish. What do you do?
options: Take it seriously with the client without conceding the person, then work with your PMA on the specific behaviours that read as junior on calls — without framing it as a client complaint about them.
Defend your PMA to the client and leave it there.
Don't mention it to your PMA — it would only damage their confidence over nothing.
Keep your PMA off that client's calls for a while.
questions.explain: Three moves at once: don't throw your PMA under the bus, don't dismiss the client, and separate the feedback from the complaint. Passing a complaint straight through is lazy leadership; extracting the coachable behaviour from it is the job. Withholding it is paternalistic — the client's perception will surface anyway.

questions.prompt: Your PMA covers for a mistake you made — quietly fixes it, tells nobody, and mentions it to you afterwards as a favour. How do you respond?
options: Thank them sincerely; it was a genuine kindness.
Thank them, and be clear that you'd rather they told you in the moment than fixed it silently — because the version where they hide their own mistakes starts here.
Tell them never to touch your work without asking.
Thank them and raise it with Matthew yourself.
questions.explain: Gratitude and a norm correction at the same time, about a genuinely kind act. It's a hard note to hit. Pure thanks misses what just got established — silent-fixing is now the pod norm. Ingratitude kills the initiative you want; escalating it makes them regret telling you.

18.title: Day 18 — Leadership II: Hiring, Training & Managing Your PMA
18.sub: Questions 15–29, continuing from yesterday. Scenario-based. ~15 min.

questions.prompt: A PMA candidate is impressive: fast, articulate, ambitious, great answers. The one thing you notice is that in every story about a difficult colleague, they come off as the reasonable one. What's the concern?
options: Nothing — that's a candidate describing themselves well in an interview.
They may lack people-smarts.
They may be overqualified and likely to leave.
They may be low on humility and high on the other two — Lencioni's most dangerous profile, and the hardest to detect later.
questions.explain: The Skillful Politician: hungry and people-smart, missing humble. They are people-smart — that's exactly what makes it work in the interview. 'Always the reasonable one' is the observable tell, and this profile is the hardest to spot once they're inside.

questions.prompt: Two finalists. One knows Meta cold but is quietly territorial about credit. The other is noticeably behind on the platform but curious, coachable, and generous. Six-month view?
options: The experienced one — you need output now, and you can coach the behaviour.
Whichever interviews better with Matthew.
The coachable one — the platform gap closes in weeks; the credit thing doesn't.
Neither; keep looking.
questions.explain: Skills are trainable on a known timeline; character isn't. A credit-hoarding PMA in a two-person pod poisons the exact trust the pod runs on. Hiring the experienced one is the standard mistake, and it sounds responsible.

questions.prompt: In week two, your new PMA hasn't asked you a single question. Should you be pleased?
options: Yes — they're independent and picking it up from the SOPs.
No. In week two, no questions almost always means they're guessing, and you should go find out what they've assumed.
Neutral — some people just work quietly.
No — you should assign harder work to force questions.
questions.explain: Silence from a new hire is a signal, not an achievement. The fix is you going to find it, not waiting for them to come — and not manufacturing pressure, which produces stress rather than surfaced assumptions.

questions.prompt: Your new PMA comes to you with a problem they should be able to solve, and you're mid-fire-drill on a client account. What's the cost of "can you figure it out and let me know?"
options: None — it's a reasonable boundary and they should be able to solve it.
None, as long as you apologise later.
Large — you should always stop for your PMA.
Small, if you say when you'll be free and follow up. Large, if this is the first time they've asked for help.
questions.explain: The answer is conditional, and that's the point. Your reaction the first time your PMA says 'I'm stuck' sets the tone for the next two years — so the same sentence costs almost nothing on the tenth ask and a great deal on the first. A retroactive apology isn't the same as a follow-through.

questions.prompt: Your PMA tells you they're overwhelmed and can't hit this week's deliverables. You look at their workload and think it's genuinely reasonable — you'd have managed it. Best response?
options: Tell them kindly that this is the volume the role requires, and help them prioritise.
Take some work back this week and reassess.
Ask them to walk you through their week hour by hour before you conclude anything.
Tell them everyone feels that way at first and it gets easier.
questions.explain: 'You'd have managed it' is not evidence. Nine times in ten the hour-by-hour reveals a broken process, an unclear priority, or something outside work — and all three have different fixes. Notice that this question asks you to distrust your own instinct. Pre-emptively removing work can also read as loss of confidence.

questions.prompt: Your PMA is performing well but tells you they want your job within a year — and you don't think they'll be ready. What do you say?
options: Encourage the ambition without commenting on the timeline.
Tell them it's up to Matthew, not you.
Tell them to focus on the current role first.
Be honest that a year looks unlikely from where they are, name specifically what the gap is, and offer to build the plan that closes it.
questions.explain: Honest, specific, supported. Vague encouragement is the failure mode here and it's the default — it's the kind answer that's actually unkind, because they'll spend twelve months assuming they're on track. Deflecting to Matthew abdicates development you own.

questions.prompt: You inherit a PMA who was, by every account, badly managed by their last PMS — cautious, defensive, checks everything twice, waits for permission. First 30 days?
options: Give them a lot of autonomy immediately to signal trust.
Talk to them about what went wrong with their last PMS so you can avoid it.
Be extremely clear and consistent about expectations, give them one thing to own outright, and be conspicuously calm the first several times something goes wrong.
Treat it as a clean slate and manage them the way you'd manage anyone.
questions.explain: Conspicuously calm the first several times is the key phrase — trust is rebuilt by demonstration, repeatedly, not by reassurance. Sudden autonomy reads as a test they're going to fail. And relitigating their old PMS with them is the gossip problem wearing a caring face.

questions.prompt: Four months of bi-weekly 1:1s. Every single time you ask "is there anything I could be doing better as a manager?", your PMA says "no, all good." What's the most likely read?
options: You're doing well — take the answer at face value.
They don't believe the question is real yet, and the fix is something you do outside the 1:1, not a better version of the question.
They're conflict-avoidant and you should press harder in the moment until they give you something.
Drop the question; it clearly isn't working for this person.
questions.explain: The question isn't the problem. Nobody tells their manager what they're doing wrong because they were asked nicely — they do it because they've watched that manager admit a mistake, take feedback without flinching, and change something. Pressing for criticism in the moment is a status test, not an invitation.

questions.prompt: A client account is on fire the morning of your PMA's 1:1. It's the second time in three months you'd be moving it. What do you do?
options: Move it — a live client issue genuinely outranks a recurring internal meeting.
Keep it but cut it to 10 minutes so you at least touch base.
Keep the slot, tell your PMA why the account matters, and use part of the 30 minutes working the fire together.
Move it, and tell them explicitly why, when you're rescheduling it to, and that it's the last time.
questions.explain: The conflict is false. A live fire is material for a 1:1 — it's coaching, it's a real obstacle, and it puts your PMA inside a problem they'd otherwise only hear about. Moving it is defensible and is how 1:1s quietly die; twice in three months is a pattern and they've noticed. Rescheduling honestly is the strong second-best.

questions.prompt: Your PMA has been producing the weekly client reports for four months. You've checked every one before it goes out. There has never been an error. Which stage are you in, and what's the problem?
options: Stage 3, and the problem is that you've never moved them to stage 4 — four months clean is the signal to hand it over outright and tell them you have.
Stage 4 already, since they're the ones doing the work.
Stage 2 — you're still involved every week, so they haven't genuinely taken it on.
No problem. Checking reporting before it reaches a client is cheap insurance.
questions.explain: Never leaving stage 3 is the most common training failure at an agency, and it's invisible because it looks diligent. Four months without an error is proof. The 'and tell them you have' half matters as much as the handover — a promotion nobody announces isn't one. And if you're still checking, it isn't stage 4 by definition.

questions.prompt: Week one with a new PMA. They need to learn how we audit an ad account and you're slammed, so you send them the SOP plus three recorded audits and ask them to produce one. Which stage did you just start at, and what's the risk?
options: Stage 1 — the recordings are you doing it while they watch, which is what stage 1 is.
Stage 2 — they're helping by producing one themselves.
Stage 4 — they're running it end to end with nobody watching.
Stage 3 with nothing behind it. Recordings aren't stage 1, because stage 1 is you narrating your reasoning live and answering their questions as they come.
questions.explain: Skipping stages 1 and 2 produces confident wrong answers. A recording is a reference document — it can't answer a question, so async material doesn't substitute for stage 1. This is the most useful thing on the page for someone busy and well-intentioned.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the answer we're actually looking for when we ask you to name something about how you'd lead a PMA that you'd be embarrassed for them to read?
options: "I avoid the conversation when I think someone will get upset, so things pile up until they're bigger than they needed to be. I'm going to raise things within 48 hours even when they feel too small to mention."
"I'm probably too much of a perfectionist, so I'd need to watch that I don't hold my PMA to an unreasonably high standard."
"I think I'd need to work on my communication and be more intentional about building trust over time."
"Honestly, nothing comes to mind — I've thought about this a lot and I'd try to lead the way I'd want to be led."
questions.explain:
What matters is honesty and specificity, not polish: a real, unflattering tendency plus a concrete change you could be held to. 'Too much of a perfectionist' is a strength in disguise. 'Work on my communication' is an abstraction with no action attached. And 'nothing comes to mind' is the one to be most suspicious of in yourself — someone who can't be candid in writing won't be candid in front of a PMA either.

You'll be asked this again as a written question in the debrief. This version only checks that you know what a real answer looks like.

19.title: Day 19 — Client Comms I: The Relationship & Communication Foundations
19.sub: The north star, proactivity, and hospitality applied to clients. ~10 min.

questions.prompt: What's the test a PMS runs before any client message or update?
options: 'What's the shortest reply I can send?'
'Can this wait until the next call?'
'If I were the client, what would I want to know — and how would I want to hear it?'
'How do I make the numbers look their best?'
questions.explain: The comms north star. Both halves matter — what they'd want to know and how they'd want to hear it.

questions.prompt: It's Tuesday. New creative went live yesterday, early numbers look good, nothing is wrong. What does a PMS do?
options: Send a short proactive update anyway — the client should never have to wonder how things are going
Nothing — no news is fine until the weekly call
Wait until there's a problem to reach out
Only update if the client asks
questions.explain: Proactivity isn't a bad-news protocol. A client who only hears from you when something is wrong learns to dread hearing from you.

questions.prompt: A client emails, 'Hey, how are the ads doing?' What does that tell a PMS?
options: Everything's fine — just reply with numbers
They don't trust us; get defensive
Nothing — clients ask that all the time
We slipped on proactivity — they shouldn't have had to ask; tighten the update cadence going forward
questions.explain: The question itself is the diagnostic. Answering it well and not changing the cadence means you'll get it again next month.

questions.prompt: In the client relationship, what's the difference between service and hospitality (Guidara)?
options: They're the same thing
Service is doing the work correctly (the media buying); hospitality is how you make the client feel while you do it — both matter, and the second is what retains them
Hospitality means always saying yes
Service is only for new clients
questions.explain: Service is competence; hospitality is the experience of being looked after. Note that hospitality is not agreeableness — saying yes to everything is neither.

questions.prompt: One client wants a quick Loom, another wants tight bullets, another wants a call. What principle guides each update?
options: Send everyone the identical standardized report
Always use whatever's fastest for you
Whatever the agency template says
One-size-fits-one — contour the format and depth to the specific person
questions.explain: One-size-fits-one. The same principle you apply to a PMA who wants detail versus one who wants the goal and room.

questions.prompt: A client mentions offhand they're nervous about an upcoming launch. The 'unreasonable hospitality' move is to…
options: Note it and move on
Wait for them to email you
Anticipate the need — send a proactive pre-launch check-in and a simple what-to-expect note before they ask
Tell them not to worry
questions.explain: The 1% lens: a small, disproportionate gesture, acted on rather than filed. 'Don't worry' addresses the feeling without addressing the cause of it.

questions.prompt: Which reflects the AdClass way to position bad news?
options: Soften it until it's vague
Honest, clear, and with a plan — early, before they're surprised by it
Delay it until you've fixed it
Bury it inside good news
questions.explain: Honest with a plan, and early. Delaying until it's fixed is the most tempting of the wrong answers, because it feels like protecting the client.

20.title: Day 20 — Client Comms II: Running the Call & Presenting Strategy
20.sub: Hard conversations, owning mistakes, and structuring an update. ~10 min.

questions.prompt: A client just had their worst month since onboarding. What's the right structure for that conversation?
options: Lead with excuses and external factors
Own it → give the diagnosis → present the turnaround plan → give a timeline; direct, not defensive
Reassure them it'll be fine, without specifics
Wait for them to bring it up
questions.explain: Own, diagnose, plan, timeline — in that order. Reassurance without specifics is the same as no plan, and the client can tell.

questions.prompt: You discover a tracking error on your side cost two weeks of clean data. What do you do?
options: Quietly fix it and hope they don't notice
Blame the CRM or Meta
Wait until the next QBR
Tell the client early — own it, explain the impact, the fix, and the timeline, and loop in your pod leader
questions.explain: Vulnerability-based trust, pointed at a client. Note the last clause — bad news travels up immediately too, so your pod leader hears it from you rather than from the client.

questions.prompt: Mid-turnaround, an anxious client is emailing daily. Best move?
options: Stop replying so they calm down
Tell them to trust the process
Be present with the worry first, then re-anchor them on the plan and timeline — and raise your proactive update cadence
Escalate them to the founder immediately
questions.explain: Daily emails are an expectations gap, and the fix is more proactive contact, not less. 'Trust the process' dismisses the feeling and gives them nothing to hold onto.

questions.prompt: A client pushes for work you can't deliver profitably or well. Best response?
options: Hold the line with reasoning — flex what you genuinely can, and escalate before conceding something you shouldn't
Say yes to keep them happy
Flatly refuse with no explanation
Ignore the request
questions.explain: Pushback with reasoning, plus a genuine flex where one exists. Saying yes to keep them happy is how a scope problem becomes a delivery problem and then a churn problem.

questions.prompt: What order makes a strategy update land best?
options: A list of everything that went wrong
All the media-buying mechanics first
Whatever comes to mind on the call
Results → what we learned → what we're doing next → what we need from you
questions.explain: Results first, because that's what they came for. Mechanics-first is the most common mistake by people who find the mechanics interesting.

questions.prompt: When is it right to pull your pod leader or Matthew into a client situation?
options: Only after it's become a crisis
Early, whenever it helps the client — asking for help is Humble, not weak
Never — handle everything yourself
Only if the client requests it
questions.explain: Escalate early, with a position. Waiting for a crisis is the version that feels like competence and costs the most.

questions.prompt: A client sends a terse, frustrated message. Best first internal move?
options: Assume they're difficult and get defensive
Match their tone
Make the charitable assumption — respond with curiosity and care, find the real concern, and address it with a plan
Delay replying until they cool off
questions.explain: Terseness is usually pressure, not hostility. The charitable assumption gets you to the real concern faster than any of the alternatives.

22.title: Day 22 — End-of-Month Examination (Part 1: Written)
22.sub: Closed-book. Written portion only — the two live-account diagnoses and verbal walkthrough happen off-app. ~40 min.

questions.prompt: Six weeks in: three angle refreshes, two new landing pages, a rebuilt offer page. Cost per lead is flat throughout. What's the conclusion, and what do you do with it?
options: The economics don't work at this price point — take it to the client as an offer conversation, not another creative test
Creative still isn't strong enough. Run a fourth refresh
Something's wrong with the pixel or the data
The structure needs rebuilding — move it to CBO
questions.explain: "If creative can't solve it, it's an economics problem." Three refreshes and two pages is enough evidence.
